newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia little affected by U.S. trade subsidy loss.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia little affected by U.S. trade subsidy loss.

text.p: Malaysia will be little affected by the United States' withdrawal of tariff subsidies under the Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) next year, economists said on Thursday.
They said the fast-growing Malaysian economy would lose a tariff advantage estimated at around 100 million ringgit ($40 million) a year calculated on the basis of its 1995 exports to the U.S.
Under the GSP, nations are allowed to export a specified list of goods at zero or subsidised rates of tariff.
"The impact will be very small. Exports under GSP account for just two percent of Malaysia's total exports," said Ghazali Atan, economist with MBf Unit Trust Management in Kuala Lumpur.
"It is not anything to be worried about. The reason why Malaysia is graduating from that category is that it has done so well," said Rajeev Malik, an economist with Jardine Fleming in Singapore.
He said some industries might briefly feel the loss of price advantage. "This will put more pressure on Malaysian companies to become competitive," Malik said.
According to the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI), Malaysia's GSP exports to the U.S. in 1995 were just 10.5 percent of total exports to that country.
It's total GSP exports last year were worth 20.8 billion ringgit against overall exports of 185.3 billion ringgit.
The Ministry said GSP exports to the European Union were 12.6 billion ringgit and to Japan about 3.3 billion.

The reactions to Malaysia's GSP status followed a news agency report from Washington that incorrectly quoted Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky as saying that Malaysia would be graduated from the GSP next week.
A U.S. Embassy spokesman told Reuters this was not true as Malaysia would move out of the system only on January 1, 1997.
"There will be a presidential proclamation issued in about a week which graduates Malaysia from this programme starting January 1, 1997," Barshefsky said in Washington.
Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said the withdrawal of GSP privileges would have little impact on Malaysian industry.

"We do realise that one day Malaysia will lose its GSP status and that is why we have always urged industries to be more efficient," Mahathir told reporters after launching Malaysia's first locally made motorcycle at Gurun in northern Perak state.
"Many of these privileges are enjoyed by American companies that have production facilities here for re-export back to the United States," he said.
Mahathir said Malaysia was increasing its trade with other countries such as China and Japan, which would further reduce the impact of the loss of GSP status.
"Singapore has gone though this stage without losing much either in GDP growth or export growth," said Liew Yin Sze, an economist with J.M.Sassoon & Co in Singapore.
Ghazali of MBf said some of these benefits would return to Malaysia in a few years as the U.S. undertook a planned reduction of duties to near zero by 1999 on two-third of the goods under the GSP.
